title: Kestrel and the Kitchen
premise: Sable Yarrow built her wedding-planning business on other people's joy precisely because she lost her own a decade ago, when she fled a small town and the man she wronged. A routine estate job lands her in Kestrel Hollow, where an orchard deed names both the town's beloved cider-maker, Jonah Vane—the man she abandoned—and the estranged half-sister she's never met, forcing the three of them into a legal and emotional standoff over land that belongs to none of them cleanly. As harvest season presses in, Sable must choose between protecting her anonymity and testifying to what really happened the night the orchard burned, a truth that could save the deed or destroy whatever fragile family is forming. She finally speaks the rehearsed sentence—her confession—at the first-press festival, and the three choose each other over the deed, rebuilding the orchard together as co-heirs of something no court can divide.
about_author: Theo Iversen is a former small-town journalist who spent five years covering county courthouse disputes before turning to fiction full-time. They write from a converted barn in the Pacific Northwest, where they keep a stubborn apple tree that refuses to stop bearing fruit.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable takes what should be a simple estate-appraisal job in Kestrel Hollow and discovers the orchard deed lists two names: Jonah Vane and a stranger named Wren Yarrow—her own surname. The beat is dread disguised as professionalism; she almost drives away but doesn't.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Perfect Weddings
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Flashback woven through present-day planning work shows why Sable quit believing in weddings after the fire ten years ago. Emotional beat: grief kept tidy, like her color-coded binders, until the orchard job cracks the lid.

chapters.title: Jonah Vane, Cider and Stone
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She visits the orchard intending to assess it anonymously and comes face to face with Jonah, who recognizes her instantly and says nothing. The beat is charged silence—two people fluent in avoidance.

chapters.title: A Sister Made of Paperwork
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren arrives in town with a lawyer's letter and a lifetime of questions about the father who never claimed her. She meets Sable without knowing who she is. Beat: wary curiosity, the ache of being someone's secret.

chapters.title: The Town That Remembers
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs via townsfolk at the general store. Gossip reconstructs fragments of the fire night for the reader while Sable listens, cornered by kindness. Beat: the horror of being known by a place you tried to erase yourself from.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah proposes a temporary truce: all three stay through harvest, then settle the deed however the courts—or their consciences—decide. Sable agrees because leaving now would confirm everything. Beat: uneasy covenant, first real conversation in a decade.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Working the orchard alongside Jonah, old intimacy resurfaces in small gestures—a steadied ladder, shared coffee. Sable deflects into planning mode, offering to organize the first-press festival. Beat: warmth she doesn't trust herself to accept.

chapters.title: What Wren Found in the Attic
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers letters proving their father knew about her all along and chose silence. She confronts Sable, who admits only that she 'knew him.' Beat: betrayal compounding betrayal; the sisters' fragile alliance strains.

chapters.title: The Fire, Part One
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Partial flashback: the night of the fire, ending on the moment before the reveal. We learn Sable was there, that someone was hurt, and that she ran before dawn. Beat: claustrophobic guilt, the reader circling the wound.

chapters.title: Festival Preparations and Small Sabotages
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. As festival planning brings the trio together, anonymous acts of vandalism hit the orchard—cut fences, salted soil. Suspicion falls on a rival cidery, but Wren wonders if it's closer to home. Beat: rising external threat mirroring internal fracture.

chapters.title: Rain on the Press House Roof
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Trapped by a storm in the press house, Jonah and Sable nearly cross the line back into love; he asks her directly what happened that night. She gives him half the truth. Beat: tenderness laced with dishonesty, the romance's highest point before its fall.

chapters.title: The Lawyer's Letter
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The rival cidery produces an old document suggesting the father sold his share before dying—meaning the deed fight may be moot and the orchard lost regardless. The three unite against a common enemy. Beat: found-family instinct firing under pressure.

chapters.title: Digging Through County Records
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Research reveals the sale was forged—by someone the night of the fire protected. Sable realizes the truth she's hiding is also the evidence that saves the orchard. Beat: the trap closing; justice requires her confession.

chapters.title: The Fire, Part Two
chapters.summary: Full flashback, Sable's POV. The complete truth: Sable's father set the fire; she helped cover for him, and Jonah's brother was injured fleeing the blaze. Her decade of exile was penance. Beat: devastating clarity; the reader finally holds the whole weight.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable writes and rewrites the confession she's rehearsed for ten years, unable to say it aloud even alone. Meanwhile Jonah, sensing her retreat, pulls away. Beat: the lowest point; love and honesty feel mutually exclusive.

chapters.title: Wren's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren learns Sable's identity from the county clerk and confronts her: confess publicly or Wren walks and takes the lawsuit with her. Beat: righteous anger from a sister who has been lied to twice over.

chapters.title: Night Before First Press
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah finds Sable standing in the burned section of the orchard at midnight. She tells him everything before she can tell anyone else. He doesn't forgive her—not yet—but he doesn't leave. Beat: raw, quiet devastation; the beginning of repair.

chapters.title: First Press Festival
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Before the whole town, Sable says the rehearsed sentence: 'I knew my father set the fire, and I let you believe otherwise.' The crowd's reaction splits; the rival cidery's forgery collapses as her testimony triggers a records investigation. Beat: cathartic public reckoning.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Apples
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the days after, the town processes the truth; some forgive, some don't. Wren and Sable begin the slow work of sisterhood, sorting their father's letters together. Beat: bruised hope; justice done imperfectly but honestly.

chapters.title: The Court's Decision
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The judge voids the forged sale and grants the deed to the three heirs jointly. Jonah offers Sable not absolution but partnership: stay, work, earn it. Beat: measured grace; love rebuilt on truth rather than nostalgia.

chapters.title: A Wedding, Finally
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable plans one last wedding—not her own, but Wren's small ceremony in the orchard—and for the first time believes in what she's building. Beat: full-circle healing; the planner becomes a participant in love.

chapters.title: Kestrel and the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, closing chapter. One year later: first true harvest, the press house full, the found family gathered in the farmhouse kitchen where the title's image completes itself. Sable stays. Beat: belonging earned, home chosen, the past tense finally released.
